THE FASTENER GUIDE, REDRAWN

Every millimetre in these renders is read from the tables already in index.html — METRIC_BOLTS, SCREW_GAUGES, WALL_PLUGS. Nothing is drawn to taste. An M6 beside an M8 is smaller by exactly the right amount, a 1.6 mm washer is thinner than a 2 mm one, and the thread you see is the real pitch: M10 coarse at 1.5 has visibly fewer turns than M10 fine at 1.0.

The page stays the light house console. The render sits in ONE dark viewport — the only dark surface in the app — because metal reads on dark and nowhere else needs to.

Pick a direction and I will build it into index.html.

A · WORKBENCH — the object is the page.

The render takes the middle, configured from the left, dimensioned on the right, with the spanner and the two drills laid out beneath at the SAME scale as the bolt above. Closest to the screenshot you shared.

Strength: the fastener is unmistakably the subject; the fit answers are read off a picture, not a table.
Cost: the widest layout — it needs the desktop. Most of the screen is given to one item.

B · THE LADDER — the size, in context.

Same render, plus a second lane: the same nut at M6, M8, M10, M12 and M16, all at true size. The step between sizes becomes a thing the eye settles rather than a number to be trusted. Under it, the whole metric table, live.

Strength: answers "is this an 8 or a 10?" — the question actually asked when a customer holds up a loose bolt.
Cost: the ladder eats 170 px that A gives to the object itself.

C · ANSWER FIRST — the sentence leads.

A plain sentence sized to be read across the room, then four big figures, then the table. The render is a tall card at the side: the proof, not the headline.

Strength: fastest to read, and the sentence is the thing that actually gets said out loud at the counter. Search stays the front door.
Cost: the render is small — the least of the three at showing an unfamiliar item to someone who does not know its name.

THE OTHER FAMILY — the same layout carrying a screw.

A number-8 black screw at 2.4:1, the red plug it fits shown IN SECTION so the bite on the ribs is visible, and the 6 mm masonry bit that makes the hole. Finish is not decoration: black phosphate and gold passivate are how the customer names the screw, so the render changes metal with the finish chip.

The plug's outside diameter IS the drill size — the one fact that stops a plug spinning — so it is drawn at exactly that.

THE PHONE — its own design, not a squeezed console.

Its headline is the thing only a phone can do: the bolt is drawn at 1:1, 3.78 px to the millimetre, with a real ruler under it. Lay the customer's bolt on the glass and step the size until the threads line up. No typing, no name needed.

The washer and nut are dropped in 1:1 mode — at life size they do not fit, and shrinking them would break the promise the badge makes.

STILL OPEN, and worth your answer:

1. Bolt HEAD TYPES — hex is drawn. Do you also need cup/carriage, csk socket, and the roofing screw with its EPDM washer? Each is real drawing work.

2. GRADE. 8.8 / 10.9 / 4.8 changes the torque figures and nothing visual except the head marking. Worth stamping the grade on the head in the render?

3. NEIGHBOURS on the phone — the ladder is desktop-only at the moment.

4. The dark viewport in DIRECT SUNLIGHT. It is the one thing I cannot test from here. If the phone is used in the yard, I would give the phone viewport a light variant.
